prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Street Yarn Roses caged in windows, heighten Your faint blooms today; Silks and sheeny satins, brighten; He has passed this way! Could ye keep his fleeting presence Gone beyond recall, But a little of his essence, I would have you all. Arabesque so quaint and shady, That mightst catch his eye To adorn a stately lady Ere her hour went by, Canst assure me that his glancing Rested on they fold? Did that set your purples dancing? Wake the sleepy gold? Ye neglected apple-venders Mouldering in the street, Did he curse between your tenders, Spurning with his feet? Then must I an alms deliver For his graceless pride; Could I buy his sins forever, I’d not be denied. Paying patiently his ransom Never conscience-pricked; Cheating Justice of her handsome Heartless derelict. Did he view thee, ancient steeple, With thy weird clock-face, Frowning down on sinful people Passing out of grace? Nay, respond not to my question With thy prate of time: Things to which my soul must hasten Lie beyond thy chime. With no circumstance to screen us, We must meet again: I shall bid God judge between us, Answering Amen.

Keywords: Street, Yarn, Roses

outputs.L1:
**Street Yarn**

Roses caged in windows,  
Heighten your faint blooms today;  
Silks and sheeny satins, brighten;  
He has passed this way.

Could ye keep his fleeting presence,  
Gone beyond recall—  
But a little of his essence—  
I would have you all.

Arabesque, so quaint and shady,  
That mightst catch his eye  
To adorn a stately lady  
Ere her hour went by,

Canst thou assure me that his glancing  
Rested on thy fold?  
Did that set your purples dancing,  
Wake the sleepy gold?

Ye neglected apple-venders,  
Mouldering in the street,  
Did he curse between your tenders,  
Spurning with his feet?

Then must I an alms deliver  
For his graceless pride;  
Could I buy his sins forever,  
I’d not be denied.

Paying patiently his ransom,  
Never conscience-pricked;  
Cheating Justice of her handsome,  
Heartless derelict.

Did he view thee, ancient steeple,  
With thy weird clock-face,  
Frowning down on sinful people  
Passing out of grace?

Nay, respond not to my question  
With thy prate of time:  
Things to which my soul must hasten  
Lie beyond thy chime.

With no circumstance to screen us,  
We must meet again;  
I shall bid God judge between us,  
Answering, Amen.
outputs.L2:
Roses made of street yarn, trapped behind panes of glass, make your pale blossoms seem more vivid today.  
Shimmering silks and glossy satins, shine more brightly—  
he has gone past here.

If you could hold even a trace of him,  
some small remnant of the presence that has vanished forever,  
I would take every one of you.

Strange, shadowed arabesque,  
perhaps you drew his glance,  
perhaps you were meant to decorate a noble woman  
before her time was finished.  
Can you promise me his eyes paused on your folds?  
Did that look make your purples tremble with life,  
and stir your dull gold awake?

You forgotten sellers of apples,  
decaying there in the street—  
did he swear as he passed your baskets,  
kicking them aside with his feet?  
If so, I must give charity  
to pay for his rude arrogance;  
if I could purchase all his sins for myself,  
nothing would stop me.

I would quietly pay the price of his redemption,  
without my conscience troubling me,  
robbing Justice of the prize  
of that handsome, pitiless outcast.

Did he look at you, old steeple,  
with your strange clock face  
scowling down upon sinners  
as they drift beyond grace?  
No—do not answer me  
with your empty talk of hours and bells.  
The things my spirit must hurry toward  
are beyond anything your chime can measure.

With nothing left to hide or shield either of us,  
we must meet once more.  
Then I will ask God to decide between us,  
and I will answer, Amen.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a speaker who moves through the street in the aftermath of a man’s passing, searching anxiously for any remaining trace of him. Even the smallest sign of his presence seems precious. The speaker longs to preserve something of the man—some mark of where he looked, what he touched, or what briefly drew his attention—as though these fragments could keep him near.

As the speaker looks around, ordinary street objects become charged with emotional meaning. The speaker questions the goods in the shops, the street vendors, and the surrounding scene, wondering whether the man noticed them or paused before them. Did he look at the displays? Did he speak to a seller? Did he leave any impression on the world around him? These questions show the speaker’s intense desire to reconstruct the man’s movements and recover a sense of intimacy through the physical details of the street.

At the same time, the poem moves beyond simple longing into a more profound moral and spiritual concern. The speaker acknowledges the man’s pride and wrongdoing, yet still expresses a willingness to pay for him, to redeem him, or to bear the cost of his sins. This willingness suggests a love that is not blind to fault but remains devoted despite it. The speaker’s desire to save the man gives the poem an emotional intensity that combines grief, love, and religious yearning.

The poem also creates a strong contrast between the visible world and the invisible spiritual reality beneath it. The street is filled with earthly signs: shop goods, vendors, passing crowds, and the church steeple rising above the scene. These details belong to daily life and to time, but they also point toward something beyond time. The church steeple, in particular, reminds the speaker that human actions and attachments are ultimately measured against eternal concerns.

By the end, the speaker looks forward to a final encounter with the man before God. This imagined meeting shifts the poem from the temporary street to the realm of divine judgment. There, earthly uncertainty will end, and God will decide between them. The speaker’s longing for traces of the man in the world thus becomes part of a larger hope: that beyond loss, sin, and pride, there will be a final reckoning in which truth and mercy are revealed.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who is haunted by the absence of a beloved man who has departed and left behind an unresolved emotional and moral burden. Rather than addressing him directly, the speaker turns to the world through which he may have passed: the street, the objects along it, the fabrics displayed in shop windows, the vendors who might have seen him, and even the church steeple rising above the town. Each of these things becomes a possible witness, as if the speaker hopes that the ordinary surroundings might preserve some trace of him or offer evidence of where he has gone.

This search is not merely physical. The beloved is remembered as morally flawed, perhaps guilty, faithless, or spiritually compromised, and the speaker’s longing is mixed with a need for judgment. The speaker wants to know not only where he went, but what his departure means: whether he can be forgiven, condemned, recovered, or understood. The fabrics and shop goods suggest the material world’s beauty and temptation, while the vendors and passersby represent human society, gossip, and limited knowledge. The steeple introduces the possibility of divine authority, yet even it stands at a distance, unable to give the speaker a direct answer.

As the poem develops, it becomes clear that no earthly witness can satisfy the speaker’s desire for certainty. The street cannot speak; the objects cannot explain; the people who may have seen the beloved cannot judge the full truth of his soul. The speaker’s longing therefore grows into a deeper spiritual demand. What is needed is not simply information, but a final reckoning—an encounter in which love, guilt, injury, and justice can all be answered.

By the end, the poem concludes that such an answer cannot be found in the visible world. Human memory, physical traces, and social judgment are all inadequate. The only meaningful resolution will come in a final meeting before God, where both the speaker and the departed beloved will be seen completely and judged truly. In this way, the poem transforms personal grief into a spiritual drama, suggesting that only divine judgment can resolve the speaker’s need for truth, justice, and reunion.
outputs.L5:
On a quiet street just after sunrise, a small basket of yarn sat beside a garden gate, its colors spilling out like a soft rainbow. Red, pink, and cream threads twisted together, catching the light as if they had been placed there by the morning itself.

Beside the basket grew a row of roses, their petals bright against the old stone wall. A woman knelt nearby, knitting slowly while the street awakened around her. Each stitch seemed to echo the gentle beauty of the flowers, as though she were weaving the roses into the yarn.

By the time neighbors began passing by, she had made a scarf filled with the colors of the garden. It was warm, delicate, and full of memory—a little piece of that peaceful street, wrapped in yarn and roses.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original poem in a late-Victorian/early-modernist style about walking through a city after a beloved man has passed by, addressing shop-window fabrics, street vendors, and a church steeple, with themes of longing, sin, judgment, and ransom.
counterfactuals.output:
**After He Passed**

O silks behind the glass, with your drowned gleams,  
Your peacock-greens, your violets dark as sin,  
Did ye not feel the wind of him go in  
Among your folds, and trouble all your dreams?  
He passed—my lord of sorrow and of grace—  
And left the street more naked than before;  
The lamps burned thin; the rain upon the door  
Was like a veil drawn down across his face.

Cry, orange-woman, cry your golden store!  
Cry, fishmonger, your silver dead on ice!  
What price the heart? what price the old device  
Of Paradise once forfeited, once more?  
Your scales are honest: weigh me grief for bread,  
And longing for a measure of cheap wine;  
Yet all your wares, and all these wants of mine,  
Seem bought and sold beneath the eyes of the dead.

O steeple, black against the bruisèd west,  
Thou finger of reproof, austere and high,  
Dost point at heaven—or accuse the sky  
That lets such beauty vanish from the breast?  
Your bells, close-mouthed, remember how they tolled;  
Your stones have heard what kneeling mouths deny:  
That love may wear the scarlet name of crime,  
And still be worth more ransom than pure gold.

For he has passed; and I, not shriven, stand  
Where his light footfall struck the common clay.  
The city darkens into judgment-day,  
Each window kindling like a witness-hand.  
If there be law, then let the law begin;  
If there be mercy, let it find me here—  
Following his shadow through the gaslit year,  
And paying with my soul the debt of sin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue poem titled “Street Yarn” that personifies roses in windows, silks, satins, apple-venders, and an ancient steeple, using archaic diction and rhymed quatrains.
counterfactuals.output:
# Street Yarn

I, ragged Night, do pace this stony lane,  
And draw my tale from gutters, gold, and grime;  
“Hearken,” I cry, “ye walls that drip with rain,  
I spin the street upon the wheel of Time.”  

The roses in the windows lean and sigh,  
Red-lipp’d coquettes behind their panes of glass;  
They whisper, “Lo, what weary souls go by,  
Yet none will woo us ere the moon shall pass.”  

The silks sweep forth with proud and rustling breath,  
Like duchesses that scorn the beggar’s plea;  
They trail their splendour over hints of death,  
And laugh, “Our sheen is all the sun men see.”  

The satins, pale as candle-flames at mass,  
Do murmur prayers in folds of silver skin;  
“Touch not,” they warn the hands that darkly pass,  
“For stain once set is covenant with sin.”  

The apple-venders, throned in market light,  
Cry, “Buy! buy! sweet moons of autumn’s store!”  
Their round-cheek’d fruit, like babes awake at night,  
Blush at the tales the hungry pavements bore.  

And yon old steeple, with his crooked crown,  
Gravely doth wag his iron tongue on high;  
“Fools,” saith he, “all your velvet falls adown—  
Only the bell hath leave to bruise the sky.”  

Then spake I, Night: “Good masters, mark my thread;  
Rose, silk, and satin, apple, tower, and stone—  
Each vaunteth life, yet all are sister’d dead,  
Unless some mortal grief become their own.”  

So here I stand, a shadow’s motley squire,  
And barter songs for pity, crust, or name;  
The street, my loom, is strung with rain and fire—  
I weave, I cry, and vanish in the same.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem imitating the style of Amy Lowell or another imagist poet, centered on urban street objects that may have briefly seen an absent lover, ending with an appeal to God’s judgment.
counterfactuals.output:
**Witnesses**

The rain-polished curb  
keeps a thin moon in its gutter—  
did your shoe break it?

A tram-rail, bright as a knife,  
runs on without speaking.

Under the street-lamp  
the newspaper twists and flutters,  
showing its black little wounds  
to the wind.

O letter-box, red-lipped,  
did you swallow her shadow?  
O door-step, worn hollow  
by a thousand indifferent feet,  
was hers among them?

The shop-window, after midnight,  
holds only hats, pearls,  
and my face—  
pale merchandise  
no one will buy.

Even the crossing-signal  
blinks and blinks  
like a tired witness  
afraid to answer.

Stones of the city,  
iron mouths, wet glass,  
you must have seen her pass—  
or seen the place  
where she did not.

If I accuse you falsely,  
if longing has made me mad,  
let the Lord judge between us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a formal rhyming poem where the speaker questions objects in a city street about whether “he” passed that way, and reflects on paying for his sins and meeting him again beyond time.
counterfactuals.output:
I asked the lamp, in rain’s diminished light,  
“Did he pass here beneath your amber flame?”  
It trembled like a conscience in the night,  
But gave no answer, only burned his name.  

I asked the stones, by countless footsteps worn,  
“Did he go by, with sorrow in his tread?”  
They kept the cold remembrance of the morn  
And sealed their silence round the living dead.  

I asked the gutter, whispering to the drain,  
“Did he lean down, or cast one glance below?”  
It bore away the city’s grief and stain,  
And murmured what no mortal ear may know.  

I asked the door, with iron on its face,  
“Did he once pause and lift his hand to thee?”  
It held the shadow of a vanished grace,  
Then closed more firmly on its mystery.  

O street of lamps, of rain, of stone, of dust,  
Bear witness if you saw his figure go;  
For I have paid in ashes and in trust  
The heavy debts that only sinners know.  

And if beyond the clocks, beyond the sun,  
Where hours fall silent and the stars resign,  
There comes a land where all lost roads are one,  
I shall meet him there, and he be mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a vintage-sounding lyrical poem with archaic words like “ye,” “thee,” and “canst,” involving shop-window roses, arabesque fabrics, neglected apple sellers, a clock-faced steeple, and a final religious reckoning.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the clock-faced steeple’s pallid eye,  
When vesper-gold lay thin on pane and stone,  
I saw shop-window roses dreaming dry,  
Their crimson hearts by candle-glimmer shown.  

“Come hither, ye,” the dusk-winds seemed to plead,  
“Behold what bloom in captive glass is kept;”  
Yet none would pause, for none had coin nor need,  
And in the gutter fallen petals slept.  

There hung arabesque fabrics, fold on fold,  
With moons and vines in Eastern wonder spun;  
They stirred like prayers the merchants never told,  
All purple dusk and threads of dying sun.  

Beside them sat the apple sellers gray,  
Neglected, bent beneath the market rain;  
Their baskets red as wounds of yesterday,  
Their weary mouths acquainted long with pain.  

O passer-by, canst thou not spare thine eyes?  
Canst thou not hear how hollow wheels complain?  
The poor grow dim beneath the painted skies,  
While silks are praised and roses bloom in vain.  

The steeple clock struck nine; its brazen tongue  
Made tremble every shutter, latch, and stall;  
And from the belfry’s shadow, coldly hung,  
There seemed a Voice that summoned one and all:  

“Ye weighed the bloom, yet not the bruisèd hand;  
Ye priced the cloth, but not the naked bone;  
Ye passed the least of these upon the land—  
Now stand, O souls, before the Judgment Throne.”  

Then roses withered, fabrics lost their flame,  
The apples rolled like sins across the square;  
And each man answered to his secret name,  
While Heaven opened—terrible and fair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
